articles.text: As an outgrowth of the discussion relative to putting in stock-yards in St. Paul, the yards at Minnesota Transfer will be enlarged and a hotel built.
articles.summary: The stock yards at Minnesota Transfer will be enlarged and a hotel built.

articles.text: There are in the United States, 14,160 newspapers. In Canada and Newfoundland, there are 679. Of those in the United States, New York state has the most, 1,577. Dakota has 309; Nevada the fewest of the states, 28, and Indian Territory, the fewest of the territories, six.
articles.summary: Newspaper counts: 14,160 in the United States, 309 of them in Dakota.

articles.text: Of all the states and territories in the Union, only California and Texas have a greater area than Dakota. Texas has 262,290, California has 155,980 and Dakota has 147,700 square miles. Dakota is more than 2,460 times as large as the district of Columbia, which has only sixty square miles.
articles.summary: Only Texas and California exceed Dakota in area.

articles.text: The Stockgrowers' Journal advocates the creation of the office of chief stock inspector; a proposition that we think will meet favorable consideration at the hands of the legislature. The inspectors are new under the direct authority of the stock commissioners; a body of men selected more for their business ability or their standing among cowmen than for their ability as officers or commanders of a body of men whose duty it is to see that laws are obeyed. In other words a man who would make a first-class commissioner, might be the poorest man in the country to organize a raid on a gang of horse thieves. The Montana stock inspectors are a very able body of men, whose work has given eminent satisfaction, but we certainly think their efficiency could be largely increased by being in charge of one competent man who has made a record of his ability on dealing with violators of the law.
articles.summary: Packard endorses the Stockgrowers' Journal's proposal for a Montana chief stock inspector to direct the inspectors against horse thieves.

articles.text: We have received several letters lately from persons interested in the tax suit between Stark and Billings counties. Briefly, the matter stands as follows—At the last session of the Dakota legislature, a bill was passed, authorizing any organized county to tax for all purposes, adjacent unorganized counties. Also it gave authority to the organized county to tax any unorganized county which was nearer to it than to any other organized county. Under this law, Stark county assessed and taxed Billings county before we were organized. The tax amounted to nearly thirteen mills of which three mills was territorial tax. All the rest was for school, bridge and road taxes &c., for Stark county. Our tax-payers readily conceded the justice of the territorial tax and have stood ready at any and all times to pay it, if it could have been separated from the other subjects for taxation under the bill. They can in no wise, however, see the justice of being taxed to pay for the schools, roads or bridges of Stark county. Naturally our tax-payers, seeing the unjustice of the law, refused to pay the tax. Stark county, being authorized by the law, as naturally took measures to collect the tax. Our citizens then met and decided to fight the collection and appointed T. R. Selmes of Mandan as attorney. Mr. Selmes gave his opinion that the law was unconstitutional and had an injunction issued on Stark county, restraining the further collection of taxes from Billings until the constitutionality of the law could be decided by the courts. This is the present status of the matter. Stark county has given every evidence of desiring fair play and will readily acquiesce in the decision which we confidently believe will be adverse to the constitutionality of the law. The case will come up at the August term of the circuit court and no matter which side wins, it will doubtless be appealed. It can then come before the supreme court in October in Deadwood or in November in Bismarck. We do not think that the case will then be appealed to the supreme court of the United States, as the territorial supreme court undoubtedly has sufficient jurisdiction over the acts of Dakota legislature. We will keep our readers constantly informed if any new points in the case that may arise.
articles.summary: Packard explains the Stark–Billings county tax suit: Billings taxpayers, represented by T. R. Selmes of Mandan, obtained an injunction against Stark county's tax collection; the case goes to the August circuit court term.

articles.headline: Strayed.
articles.text:
On June 10th, from Dickinson, a dark chestnut Oregon pony, weighing about 830 pounds. He had long picket rope when last seen. Branded inverted open A (thusV) on left hip. About six years old. Ten dollars reward for recovery. Address,

D. Woodward,
Dickinson, Dak.
articles.summary: D. Woodward of Dickinson offers $10 reward for a chestnut Oregon pony that strayed June 10.

articles.text: Some of the Texas drives are in a bad fix at present. There is not enough grass and water on the trail provided by Congrass and new trails are being sought. To this the neighboring cowmen are naturally objecting. They will even prevent driving on a new trail by force of arme. One of the Hashknife drives under charge of Col. Simpson was stopped near Springer, New Mexico, and there was no way out of the difficulty except to ship. The cattle were in poor condition when started and the delay on the road is likely to be serious.
articles.summary: Texas trail drives lack grass and water; a Hashknife drive under Col. Simpson was stopped near Springer, New Mexico.

articles.text: Grass is growing as well as it has this year since the first week or two it started. This does not mean an abundance of hay, but with a good deal of rustling, it probably means that enough can be secured to feed a few horses and cows on each ranch.
articles.summary: Grass is growing again, though hay will be scarce.

articles.text: The Ref. Car Co. has so far gathered about 3,200 of the 4,800 steers turned loose last season. As all of the eastern and southern and one or two of the western round-ups are yet to be heard from, the figures indicate that almost all will be gathered.
articles.summary: The Refrigerator Car Co. has gathered about 3,200 of 4,800 steers turned loose last season.

articles.text: The eastern round-up north of the track is now at work and finding large numbers of cattle. The report comes in that one round-up on Green river contained 4,000 head. This may be exaggreated but is an indication of the large number that have strayed off to the east.
articles.summary: The eastern round-up north of the track is finding many strayed cattle; one Green river round-up reportedly held 4,000 head.

articles.text: The round-up on Reynolds Bros'. range only lasted three days. It was understood that it was to extend to the Big Missouri if necessary. There are undoubtedly some cattle in that district which have never been rounded up and it would be advantageous for our regular round-up No. 6 to have this territory included in its boundaries.
articles.summary: The round-up on Reynolds Bros.' range lasted only three days; Packard urges adding that district to round-up No. 6.

articles.text: The Chicago correspondent of the Texas L. S. Journal, estimates that there will be 325,000 Texas and 210,000 northwestern cattle on the Chicago market this year. Last year there were nearly 300,000 Texans and a few over 200,000 from the northwest. 1884 saw the largest shipment, there being then 358,374 from Texas and 231,879 from the northwest.
articles.summary: Estimates of Texas and northwestern cattle receipts at Chicago for 1886.

articles.text: Beginning to-day and lasting for three days, Devil's Lake will treat itself to a blooded stock show. The tributary country has probably been filled up more rapidly with pure blood stock than any corresponding district in the west. Many wealthy farmers have gone extensively into the business of raising blooded cattle and J. J. Hill's liberality has put pure bred animals upon almost farmer's land. It will probably be as fine a stock show as the northwest has yet seen.
articles.summary: A three-day blooded stock show opens at Devil's Lake.

articles.text: J. A. Van Eeghen and Joe McCoul returned yesterday from their western trip after horses. "Van" bought between two and three hundred mostly mares and Joe about twenty. The horses are of all kinds and a few of them are for sale. They were bought in Beaverhead Co. Montana, on the Idaho line and have been on the trail for six weeks. There was good feed and water the last of the way and they arrived here in better condition than when they started.
articles.summary: J. A. Van Eeghen and Joe McCoul returned with some 200–300 horses bought in Beaverhead County, Montana.

articles.text: "Spearfish," one of the Maltese Cross horses took a trip Tuesday evening that may shorten his days considerably. He jerked away from his rider, Mike Seitz, and ran along the railroad track to the approach of the bridge. Here he tripped on his rope and as he was going at full speed, a somersault off the approach was the result. He lit square on his back on the ground beneath, a distance of over twenty feet. He was immediately ridden to the ranch and apparently did not suffer much from his fall.
articles.summary: "Spearfish," a Maltese Cross horse, broke from rider Mike Seitz and fell over twenty feet off the railroad bridge approach, apparently without much harm.

articles.headline: Fatal Disease in Colorado Camps.
articles.text: There are plenty of strange cases in the catalogue of every doctor's personal experience. I ran across several some years ago in one af the mountain camps of Colorado, all fatal, and which while bearing a certain degree of resemblance, have not been to my knowledge described as a type in any of the medical journals. At the post mortem we discovered in every instance a hard, foreign body directly in the rear of the right external iliac fossa or outer surface of the hip bone. The foreign body extended downward and varied in length from six to eight inches, the end being tubular in form and terminating in a round, honeycombed structure containing from five to seven separate cells. Singular, wasn't it. By the way, each one of these cells contained a 45-caliber, center-fire cartridge, and the entire foreign body was technically known as a Colt's revolver. These cases were very common in Colorado and the mortality resulting from them was considerable.—[Dr. G. P. Reynolds.
articles.summary: Clipped humorous item by Dr. G. P. Reynolds: the fatal "foreign body" in Colorado mining-camp corpses was a Colt's revolver.

articles.headline: Life on the Range.
articles.text: Your outfit, or bed, clothing or equipments, will cost you about half your earnings, and if you smoke freely and do not try to same your money, the end of the season will leave you neither richer nor poorer. You will often have a wet bed, and thank heaven for getting to it, wet as it is. You will always be up before daylight, and generally two hours out of the night as well; you will eat [coarse?] food—everything [fried?] in lard; [you?] will be in the [saddle?] from twelve to eighteen hours every day; you will often suffer for the want of food and water during a long day's work in hot sun; you will expose yourself to some peril of life and more of limb; you will be for much of the time as absolutely cut off from the civilized world as if you were only a vessel in mid-ocean. You will vow three times a day that when you strike the ranch again you will quit. You will be sore and bruised, cold at night, and scorched by day, wet to the skin one hour and parched with thirst the next, and for the rest of your life you will look back to your life on the range, with longing thoughts of its charms. Very few men are rich enough to indulge the taste for riding by keeping more than two saddle horses. A 'puncher' often rides a dozen, and does much of his work at full run. He breathes the finest air on earth, eats beef as freely as an ordinary workingman eats cabbage and potatoes, and fancies tne class to which he belongs are the aristocracy of labor. He is generous, always quick to appreciate pluck and kindness in others, chivalrous to the few women he sees, ever ready to help hang a horse thief, and undergoes more hardship and danger than a dozen soldiers.—[San Francisco Chronicle.
articles.summary: Clipped San Francisco Chronicle sketch of the hardships and charms of a cowboy's life.

articles.headline: Alfalfa.
articles.text:
This clover, which goes under several names, is decidedly the coming forage plant of the west, not only on account of its nutritious properties either green or cured, but on account of its adaptability to any soil and climate.

It loves water and grows best when supplied with a liberal amount, but it hangs on with a pertinacity during a long drouth that throws Aunt Jemima's plaster in the ground.

In our valley the usual time for planting is in August, which gives the young plants time to become well rooted before the cold weather comes on. Others prefer to plant in the spring after all danger of frost is over, but they do not expect to reap any benefit from the first year's crop, whereas the fall planting gives a very nice return. The third year, however, is the time we expect the best results, but as intimated above, its staying qualities are immense, and after eight and ten years of neglect, if ploughed with light plows and watered, it will come up in the most sprightly manner. You would think it had been making use of the "bloom of youth."

In preparing the land it should be well ploughed with two strong mules or horses, well harrowed and then thoroughly irrigated, and as soon as the land is dry enough sow your seed, about twelve or fifteen pounds per acre, and harrow in.

The first crop will be light and pretty full of weeds, but they never make a second attempt to outgrow their competitor, but throw up the sponge in despair, and once alfalfa becomes well rooted it will not brook any opposition, but smothers out everything else. The depth the roots will go down into mother earth in search of moisture is something marvelous, often fifteen to twenty feet, and will grow as large as a man's wrist. It is, therefore, rather hard to eradicate from your garden and orchard, and should not be allowed to seed, as it springs up wherever a seed is dropped, even after having been used as food by our domestic animals. It can be easily killed, however, when it is desired, by being flooded with water for a few days, and then the full force of a July or August sun soon kills it.

The first cutting is usually about the 10th or 15th of May owing to a late or early spring, and if there is plenty of water to irrigate during the summer one can safely rely on three, and often four, cuttings during the season. From three-fourths to a ton, and on our best lands a ton and a half, can be had at each cutting. The ground can then be used for pasturage during the winter months. If there should be a rather thin stand it is advisable to allow the clover mature its seed before cutting, as it will give a good stand afterwards, but it is not best to have the plants too thick on the ground, as better results are obtained where only a good stand is on the ground. The usual time for cutting is when the plant is in full bloom.

Alfalfa is so hardy that many have obtained the best results by simply sowing the seed broadcast in among the corn in August or September, and simply by cutting down the corn stalks with a hoe and leveling the ground when very uneven and irrigating afterwards.

We propose in our next to give some information as to the method of curing, price, baling and our market for alfalfa, and land best adapted to its growth.—[The Two Republics.
articles.summary: Clipped article from The Two Republics on planting, cutting and the hardiness of alfalfa as a western forage crop.

articles.text: 122 in the sun!
articles.summary: Temperature of 122 in the sun.

articles.text: Northern Pacific preferred stocks, 59; common, 26⅝.
articles.summary: Northern Pacific stock quotations.

articles.text: The river is as low as we have seen it in the last three years.
articles.summary: The Little Missouri is the lowest in three years.

articles.text: School will begin next Monday with Miss Alice Ellison, sister of C. F. Ellison, as teacher.
articles.summary: School will open Monday with Miss Alice Ellison as teacher.

articles.text: About fifteen hundred Bad Lands cattle were driven over from the Yellowstone round-up.
articles.summary: About 1,500 Bad Lands cattle were driven over from the Yellowstone round-up.

articles.text: Willis Eaton has finished his assessment and will make his returns to the commissoners next Monday.
articles.summary: Assessor Willis Eaton has finished the assessment and will report Monday.

articles.text: Fred Willard started for Spearfish Sunday. He will return as soon as possible with his wife and Fred Jr.
articles.summary: Fred Willard left Sunday for Spearfish to bring back his wife and son.

articles.text: The Marquise de Mores and a hunting party are down the river. Bear hunting is the principal object of the trip.
articles.summary: The Marquise de Morès and a hunting party are down the river after bear.

articles.text: Miss Jennie Morton of South Heart, was married last week to a fireman whose name we are unable to learn.
articles.summary: Miss Jennie Morton of South Heart married a fireman last week.

articles.text: Geo. E. Cole has returned from his eastern trip, having made a flying visit to his old home and other points of interest.
articles.summary: Geo. E. Cole has returned from a trip east.

articles.text: Tom Mathews, stock-inspector at Glendive is taking Fred Willard's place as inspector at the slaughter-house, during the latter's absence.
articles.summary: Glendive stock inspector Tom Mathews is substituting for Fred Willard at the slaughter-house.

articles.text: The Marquis de Mores has gone to Powder river to look up some of the cross Y steers and other business matters. Dick Moore accompanied him.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Morès, with Dick Moore, went to Powder river after cross Y steers.

articles.text: Frank Foster and wife arrived in Medora last Thursday evening. With them came a force of butchers, including "Shorty" and Cranston of last year's men.
articles.summary: Frank Foster and wife arrived with a force of butchers.

articles.text: Four-year-olds are considerably livelier than threes, as is evidenced by the fact that two steers jumped the eight-foot corral fence, a feat that has hitherto been deemed impossible.
articles.summary: Two four-year-old steers jumped the eight-foot corral fence.

articles.text: At four o'clock yesterday afternoon the [thermometer?] stood at 118 in the sun. The rain of the morning barely wet the ground and did but little to relieve the intense heat.
articles.summary: The thermometer reached 118 in the sun; morning rain gave little relief.

articles.text: C. A. Quigley, representing Studebaker Bros. M'f'g. Co., stopped off in Medora Wednesday. He reports sales of $50,000 on the N. P. between St. Paul and Helena for the last eight months.
articles.summary: Studebaker representative C. A. Quigley stopped in Medora.

articles.text: Word comes from Mingusville that Mr. and Mrs. John Munro are rejoicing over advent of a lively infant who will go through this world's trials and tribulations under the name of William.
articles.summary: A son, William, was born to Mr. and Mrs. John Munro at Mingusville.

articles.text: Dick Carr has not as yet recovered his mules, which strayed away from south of the Black Hills about two months ago. A sharp lookout by our cattlemen may bring them to light, as they are liable to come back to the Bad Lands.
articles.summary: Dick Carr's mules, strayed two months ago south of the Black Hills, are still missing.

articles.text: Dr. Jorgens and Johnny Fitzgerald started the first of the week for the Doctor's Cave Hills ranch, with two loads of supplies. They will return in a few days. The Dr. and his family will spend the most of the time until fall on the ranch.
articles.summary: Dr. Jorgens and Johnny Fitzgerald took supplies to the doctor's Cave Hills ranch.

articles.text: Eli Mickelson returned Tuesday from his trip to the Hills. He was in Rapid City the most of the time and reports that there was plenty of work, but about seven men for every job. All the boys who went from here have secured work, however.
articles.summary: Eli Mickelson returned from Rapid City reporting more men than jobs.

articles.text: There may be no connection between Fred Willard's departure for Spearfish and the threat of the Stockgrowers' Journal to come down with a deputy sheriff, a double barrelled shot-gun and a yellow dog to collect Fred's advertising bill for the editor of that paper, but we look for gore on his return.
articles.summary: Packard jokes about the Stockgrowers' Journal's threat to collect Fred Willard's advertising bill.

articles.text: The story of the shooting affray at the [E6?] ranch in which a cowboy named Chadwick was killed, was exploded by Russ Wilson on a recent trip to the Hills. He said that Chadwick and his alleged murderer were a hundred miles apart on the day the shooting was said to have occurred and that Chadwick is now alive and well.
articles.summary: Russ Wilson reports that the cowboy Chadwick, said to have been killed at a ranch shooting, is alive.

articles.text: A baby boy was born to Mrs. John Goodall last Thursday. Johnny don't say much, but feels about seven inches taller than usual. We happen to be one of the few unfortunates who were absent at the general distribution of cigars. This may be considered as an item of news or a hint, at the pleasure of the reader, however.
articles.summary: A son was born to Mr. and Mrs. John Goodall.

articles.text: Work began at the slaughter-house promptly on time this morning. The beef is in far better condition than it was this time last year; in fact it will sell readily anywhere. Layers of fat in most cases, completely cover the carcasses. The coolers have just been filled with 300 tons of ice and under the able superintendence of Frank Foster, everything is running as smoothly as at the end of the season's work last fall. About fifty head will be slaughtered to-day.
articles.summary: The Medora slaughter-house opened its season under Frank Foster, killing about fifty head the first day.

articles.text: We have an over-stock of [3⅛?] Studebaker wagons that the Studebaker M'f'g. Co. have instructed us to close out at $75 each. These wagons have never turned a wheel under a load, are new and first-class in every respect, have the Co's. full guarantee for 5,000 pounds, according to old freighters are the best ironed and easiest running wagon of its size in the world, and cost at the factory, $87 each in car lots. There never has been and never will be again such a bargain in wagons in this country. The $75 rate is cash of course and holds good for one or more. For further particulars, call at or address the Cow Boy office.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy office offers surplus Studebaker wagons at $75 each.

Brand: Lemoyne Cattle Co. (Limited), D. K. Wade, Manager, Medora — LC; ranch Tepee bottom, range Little Missouri S of R.R.; also DW
Brand: Soho Cattle Co., Chas. Eaton, Manager, Medora — SO; range Little Missouri river and Beaver [creek?] north of N.P.R.R.

Brand: Chimney Butte Ranch, Theodore Roosevelt, Proprietor; Ferris & Merrifield, Managers, P.O. Medora — Maltese cross; range six miles S of N.P.R.R. on Little Missouri
Brand: Bullion Creek Horse Ranch, Jack Bullion, Prop., Medora — SS; range Bullion creek twenty miles S of Medora
Brand: N. P. Refrigerator Car Co., Medora — cross Y; also steers purchased of Mason & Lovell; ranges Little Missouri river and Beaver creek
Brand: Ætna Ranch, Osborne Bros., Proprietors, P.O. Medora — Æ; range Knutson creek

articles.summary: Directory of display advertisements and cattle and horse brand ads on page 4, including Roosevelt's Chimney Butte Ranch brand.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Marquise de Morès leads a bear hunt down the river
events.summary: The Marquise de Morès and a hunting party were down the Little Missouri, chiefly after bear.
events.excerpt: The Marquise de Mores and a hunting party are down the river. Bear hunting is the principal object of the trip.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Marquis de Morès goes to Powder River after cross Y steers
events.summary: The Marquis de Morès went to Powder River, accompanied by Dick Moore, to look up some cross Y steers and other business.
events.excerpt: The Marquis de Mores has gone to Powder river to look up some of the cross Y steers

events.date_basis: "Tuesday evening" before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Maltese Cross horse "Spearfish" falls from railroad bridge approach
events.summary: "Spearfish," one of the Maltese Cross horses, jerked away from rider Mike Seitz, ran along the railroad track and somersaulted more than twenty feet off the bridge approach, landing on his back; he was ridden to the ranch apparently not much hurt.
events.excerpt: "Spearfish," one of the Maltese Cross horses took a trip Tuesday evening that may shorten his days considerably.

events.date_basis: "this morning" = issue date Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Medora slaughter-house opens its 1886 season
events.summary: Work began at the slaughter-house on time; the beef was fat and in far better condition than a year earlier, coolers held 300 tons of ice, and about fifty head were to be killed the first day under Frank Foster.
events.excerpt: Work began at the slaughter-house promptly on time this morning.

events.date_basis: "last Thursday evening" before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Frank Foster and butchers arrive for slaughter season
events.summary: Frank Foster and his wife arrived in Medora with a force of butchers, including "Shorty" and Cranston from the previous year.
events.excerpt: Frank Foster and wife arrived in Medora last Thursday evening.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Tom Mathews substitutes as slaughter-house inspector
events.summary: Glendive stock inspector Tom Mathews took Fred Willard's place as inspector at the slaughter-house while Willard was away.
events.excerpt: Tom Mathews, stock-inspector at Glendive is taking Fred Willard's place as inspector at the slaughter-house

events.date_basis: "Sunday" before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Fred Willard leaves for Spearfish
events.summary: Fred Willard left for Spearfish to bring back his wife and Fred Jr.
events.excerpt: Fred Willard started for Spearfish Sunday.

events.date_basis: "next Monday" after Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Medora school to open with Alice Ellison as teacher
events.summary: School was to begin the following Monday with Miss Alice Ellison, sister of C. F. Ellison, as teacher.
events.excerpt: School will begin next Monday with Miss Alice Ellison, sister of C. F. Ellison, as teacher.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Willis Eaton completes county assessment
events.summary: Assessor Willis Eaton finished his assessment and was to make his returns to the county commissioners the following Monday.
events.excerpt: Willis Eaton has finished his assessment and will make his returns to the commissoners next Monday.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Bad Lands cattle driven home from Yellowstone round-up
events.summary: About fifteen hundred Bad Lands cattle were driven over from the Yellowstone round-up.
events.excerpt: About fifteen hundred Bad Lands cattle were driven over from the Yellowstone round-up.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Three-day round-up on Reynolds Bros.' range
events.summary: The round-up on Reynolds Bros.' range lasted only three days; the paper suggested regular round-up No. 6 should take in that district toward the Big Missouri.
events.excerpt: The round-up on Reynolds Bros'. range only lasted three days.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Eastern round-up finds large numbers of strayed cattle
events.summary: The eastern round-up north of the railroad was at work finding many cattle; one round-up on Green river reportedly held 4,000 head.
events.excerpt: The report comes in that one round-up on Green river contained 4,000 head.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Refrigerator Car Co. gathers 3,200 of its steers
events.summary: The (Northern Pacific) Refrigerator Car Co. had gathered about 3,200 of the 4,800 steers turned loose the previous season.
events.excerpt: The Ref. Car Co. has so far gathered about 3,200 of the 4,800 steers turned loose last season.

events.date_basis: "yesterday" before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Van Eeghen and McCoul bring in horses from Montana
events.summary: J. A. Van Eeghen and Joe McCoul returned from Beaverhead County, Montana, after six weeks on the trail with two to three hundred horses, mostly mares, some for sale.
events.excerpt: "Van" bought between two and three hundred mostly mares and Joe about twenty.

events.date_basis: "yesterday afternoon" before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Heat reaches 118 in the sun at Medora
events.summary: At four o'clock the thermometer stood at 118 in the sun; the morning's rain barely wet the ground. A separate item noted 122 in the sun.
events.excerpt: At four o'clock yesterday afternoon the [thermometer?] stood at 118 in the sun.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Little Missouri at its lowest in three years
events.summary: The river was as low as the paper had seen it in three years.
events.excerpt: The river is as low as we have seen it in the last three years.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Grass recovering but hay will be short
events.summary: Grass was growing as well as at any time that year, though hay would not be abundant; with rustling, ranches might cut enough for a few horses and cows.
events.excerpt: Grass is growing as well as it has this year since the first week or two it started.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Steers jump eight-foot corral fence
events.summary: Two four-year-old steers jumped an eight-foot corral fence, a feat previously thought impossible.
events.excerpt: two steers jumped the eight-foot corral fence, a feat that has hitherto been deemed impossible.

events.date_basis: "Wednesday" before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Studebaker agent C. A. Quigley visits Medora
events.summary: C. A. Quigley of Studebaker Bros. Mfg. Co. stopped off in Medora, reporting $50,000 in sales along the Northern Pacific in eight months.
events.excerpt: C. A. Quigley, representing Studebaker Bros. M'f'g. Co., stopped off in Medora Wednesday.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Cow Boy office closes out Studebaker wagons at $75
events.summary: The Cow Boy office, as Studebaker agent, offered surplus 3⅛ Studebaker wagons at $75 cash each, against a factory cost of $87.
events.excerpt: We have an over-stock of [3⅛?] Studebaker wagons that the Studebaker M'f'g. Co. have instructed us to close out at $75 each.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Son William born to the John Munros at Mingusville
events.summary: Mr. and Mrs. John Munro of Mingusville had a son, named William.
events.excerpt: Mr. and Mrs. John Munro are rejoicing over advent of a lively infant

events.date_basis: "last Thursday" before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Son born to Mr. and Mrs. John Goodall
events.summary: A baby boy was born to Mrs. John Goodall; the paper joked that it missed the distribution of cigars.
events.excerpt: A baby boy was born to Mrs. John Goodall last Thursday.

events.date_basis: "last week" before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Jennie Morton of South Heart marries
events.summary: Miss Jennie Morton of South Heart was married to a fireman whose name the paper could not learn.
events.excerpt: Miss Jennie Morton of South Heart, was married last week to a fireman

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Geo. E. Cole returns from the East
events.summary: Geo. E. Cole returned from an eastern trip that included a visit to his old home.
events.excerpt: Geo. E. Cole has returned from his eastern trip

events.date_basis: "the first of the week" before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Dr. Jorgens hauls supplies to his Cave Hills ranch
events.summary: Dr. Jorgens and Johnny Fitzgerald set out with two loads of supplies for the doctor's Cave Hills ranch, where the doctor and family would spend most of the time until fall.
events.excerpt: Dr. Jorgens and Johnny Fitzgerald started the first of the week for the Doctor's Cave Hills ranch

events.date_basis: "Tuesday" before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Eli Mickelson returns from the Black Hills
events.summary: Eli Mickelson came back from Rapid City, reporting plenty of work but about seven men for every job; all the Medora men who went had found work.
events.excerpt: Eli Mickelson returned Tuesday from his trip to the Hills.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Reported killing of cowboy Chadwick proves false
events.summary: Russ Wilson, back from the Hills, said the cowboy Chadwick, reported killed in a shooting at a ranch, was alive and had been a hundred miles from his alleged murderer that day.
events.excerpt: Chadwick is now alive and well.

events.date_basis: "about two months ago" before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Dick Carr's mules stray south of the Black Hills
events.summary: Dick Carr's mules, which strayed from south of the Black Hills about two months earlier, had not been recovered; cattlemen were asked to watch for them.
events.excerpt: Dick Carr has not as yet recovered his mules

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Cow Boy teases Stockgrowers' Journal over Willard's bill
events.summary: Packard joked that the Stockgrowers' Journal had threatened to send a deputy sheriff, a shotgun and a yellow dog to collect Fred Willard's advertising bill.
events.excerpt: we look for gore on his return.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Status of the Stark–Billings county tax suit
events.summary: The Cow Boy explained that Billings County taxpayers, through attorney T. R. Selmes of Mandan, had obtained an injunction stopping Stark County from collecting taxes it levied on Billings before organization; the case was set for the August circuit court term.
events.excerpt: Our citizens then met and decided to fight the collection and appointed T. R. Selmes of Mandan as attorney.

events.date_basis: "the August term of the circuit court"
events.title: Tax suit to be heard at August circuit court
events.summary: The Stark–Billings tax case was expected at the August circuit court term, with appeal likely to the territorial supreme court.
events.excerpt: The case will come up at the August term of the circuit court

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 1 Jul 1886
events.title: Cow Boy offers Huffman's round-up photographs
events.summary: The Cow Boy advertised its remaining sets of Huffman's thirty-six instantaneous round-up photographs at $5, or $6 with a year's subscription.
events.excerpt: We have remaining a few sets of Huffmann's instantaneous round-up views

events.date_basis: "June 10th" stated
events.title: Pony strays from Dickinson
events.summary: D. Woodward of Dickinson offered $10 for a dark chestnut Oregon pony branded with an inverted open A that strayed on June 10.
events.excerpt: On June 10th, from Dickinson, a dark chestnut Oregon pony
